dedupe_keys.name: puerto rico vegetative disaster debris management after hurricanes irma and maria trees trash and hurricanes

description: This case study examines how vegetative debris from Hurricanes Irma and Maria in 2017 was managed in Puerto Rico, and proposes a theory called the Chain of Powerful Actors to explain the outcome. The authors, from US and Puerto Rican universities, released it as a preprint on SSRN, and a version appears in the International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction. The research interviewed 28 people from sectors involved in vegetative debris management, including federal and municipal government agencies, businesses, advocacy organisations and a university. Coverage is Puerto Rico. The preprint is free to read on SSRN; the journal version is behind a paywall, and no reuse licence is stated. Caveats: findings are qualitative and rest on a small set of interviews, and debris quantities are not analysed. The study found that disaster management policies and priorities left stakeholders in the island's circular economy without access to vegetative debris, that excessive vegetative debris entered Puerto Rico's limited landfill and dumpsite capacity, and that misaligned priorities weakened local capacity and reinforced dependence on federal agencies. Simulation uses: informing debris management and landfill capacity scenarios in hurricane recovery models and the rules governing debris flows. Related records: the RAND Puerto Rico health and social services assessment (case_study-puerto-rico-maria-health-social-services-recovery) covers the same event and the EPA disaster debris recovery tool (data-epa-disaster-debris-recovery-tool) lists debris facilities.
